tldr: The Oregon Farm Bureau (Angela Bailey, President) argues that agriculture is Oregon's underappreciated economic engine—generating $42 billion annually, 692,000 jobs, and 13% of GSP—yet the Prosperity Roadmap overlooks it. While praising the roadmap's commitment to permitting reform and business-friendly policy, the Farm Bureau urges the state to reduce regulatory and tax burdens on agriculture, a non-mobile, multi-generational industry where 69% of farmers operate at a net cash loss. They advocate integrating agriculture into sector strategies, applying FastTrack permitting to ag projects, supporting processing capacity, reforming the CAT, and treating farmland as productive infrastructure.

bullets.text: Oregon agriculture generates more than $42 billion in annual economic activity, supports more than 692,000 jobs statewide, and accounts for roughly 13% of gross state product.
Oregon farmers and ranchers manage more than 15 million acres of working land with approximately 96% family-owned and operated; 30,000+ farms exist, with the majority between 10 and 50 acres.
Nearly 69% of Oregon farmers report operating at a net cash loss; approximately 77% of farm household income comes from off-farm sources.

Oregon is the second most agriculturally diverse state in the nation, producing more than 220 commodities with farm-gate value exceeding $6 billion; agriculture drives more than $2.5 billion in annual exports.
More than 1,235 farms and ranches have remained in the same family for at least 100 years; 47 operations have more than 150 years of continuous family ownership.

Farm Bureau recommends explicitly identifying production agriculture as a priority sector and ensuring agriculture is represented in implementation bodies, including the Governor's Prosperity Council.

Farm Bureau calls for reform of the Corporate Activity Tax (CAT) and federal tax disconnect provisions, and urges revision of estate tax and succession policies to support multi-generational farm continuity.

Farm Bureau advocates applying permitting reform and FastTrack concepts to agricultural projects, adopting risk-based regulatory approaches, and prioritizing investment in Oregon State University Extension and agricultural research.
